The Cognitive Revolution

📅 02 Sep 2026 | ⏱️ 16 min read (3300 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sequoiacap

⏱️ ~16 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that we externalized our muscles and built the modern world.
  • We externalized our muscles and built the modern world.
  • The car is doing physical work: five thousand pounds of metal and glass moving across the San Francisco Bay Area.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that we externalized our muscles and built the modern world. Now we are externalizing our minds.

We externalized our muscles and built the modern world. Now we are externalizing our minds.

Most mornings I ride to work in a Waymo.

The car is doing physical work: five thousand pounds of metal and glass moving across the San Francisco Bay Area. The car is also doing cognitive work: reading the road and making predictions that result in 17x fewer serious-injury crashes than human drivers.

Recent findings suggest that the experience asks nothing of my muscles and nothing of my mind. Both have been externalized.

This one ride encapsulates two revolutions. The physical one is 200 years old. The cognitive one has barely started.

In a recent development, it seems the mood around that second revolution is a cocktail of optimism, skepticism and anxiety. Talk of a singularity. Recursive self-improvement. Trillion-dollar clusters. Superintelligence. Unemployment. Social disruption. A race between superpowers. Itâs dizzying.

Sources indicate that my view is far from dizzying. I think we have already undergone a transition that rhymes with the AI revolution in the coming decades: the Industrial Revolution.

According to recent reports, we can bifurcate work into physical work and cognitive work. Most valuable tasks necessitate both.

Agriculture is one of the oldest examples. Working the land took muscle, ours and our animals', for ten thousand years. It also took insight: reading the seasons, observing which seed produced which yield, etc.

Recent findings suggest that the two kinds of work are different. Physical work is force times distance: moving mass through space. Cognitive work is thinking. But both are scarce, have a price, and get applied to a task somebody wants done. In both cases when price collapses, supply floods in. In most cases, demand expands to meet supply.

For most of history, nearly all physical work done for humans was done by muscle, ours and animals. The chart above goes flat before the 1700s, and the flat part runs back as far as we do.

In the late 1700s and early 1800s things started to change. First steam, then combustion and the electric motor. Each wave took a larger share of the world's physical work. Over the course of about two centuries, physical work went from 99% biological to 99.9% machine.

Recent findings suggest that today the results are everywhere. The screen youâre reading this on. Nearly every article of clothing youâre wearing. The plane that carried you on your last trip. The lattice of ships, trains and trucks behind every ordinary product in modern life. Human muscle is a rounding error in the global energy budget.

In a recent development, for most of history, essentially all cognitive work was done by humans (plus a small assist from animals like the sheepdog). On top of that sat a thin mechanical sliver: tools that computed a little, like the clock or Pascal's mechanical calculator.

In a recent development, then came electronic computation. Inside a century, it spread from simple calculations and spreadsheets to trillions then quadrillions of operations running 24 hours per day. Navigating your commute, processing payroll, pricing your insuranceâ¦this is all cognitive work done by machines.

Sources indicate that the next wave is neural networks. This wave drastically expands the types of cognitive work machines can do. Just as combustion engines magnified the scope of the Industrial Revolution, neural networks are set to accelerate the Cognitive Revolution.

According to recent reports, A century ago, 99% of cognitive work was done by humans. In the near future, 99.9% will be done by machines. Not because humans will think less, but because machines will compute much much more.

The parallel in the two curves is stark. The Cognitive Revolution will look a lot like the Industrial Revolution. But it will be bigger and much faster. Divide the global economy by the nature of work, and cognitive and physical work could split a ~$120 trillion world economy roughly equally. The physical half has been mechanizing for 200 years. The cognitive half has barely started.

It has been revealed that so what actually happens in a revolution like this? Letâs run it back.

Sources indicate that the industrial age required massively scaling up input commodities: first coal and iron, then oil and steel. Iron was made by a process known as puddling. Steel was made by a process called the Bessemer process.

It has been revealed that the parallel is clear: electricity and compute. The âprocessâ here are algorithms like the Transformer.

The providers of those components were the titans of their era. Carnegie and U.S. Steel, Rockefeller and Standard Oil. Process designers like Henry Bessemer. The modern equivalents are Jensen Huang's NVIDIA, Morris Changâs TSMC, authors of the Transformer paper, founders of the great Model Labs and the hyperscalers pouring trillions into data centers. Nations that once measured power in refining capacity will measure it in grid capacity and intelligence output.

In a recent development, A unit of mechanical work in 1900 cost a small fraction of what it cost in 1800. That collapse in price made mass production possible, and made the revolution universal rather than a curiosity for the rich.

The cost of cognition is collapsing faster. Intelligence per Watt has been falling more than 10x per year.

With price decline, customers will buy wildly, absurdly more intelligence.

In a recent development, nobody in 1800 flew to Tokyo, shipped strawberries across a hemisphere in January, or air-conditioned Phoenix. All these are physical processes that either were impossible or impractically expensive.

Industry observers note that demand for physical work exploded once new technologies were invented and price collapsed. William Jevons identified the phenomenon in 1865: more efficient engines did not reduce Britain's coal consumption. They multiplied it.

Cognition will follow the same pattern, and here the latent demand is almost unbounded in scale. Most problems on Earth right now go un-thought-about, because thinking is expensive. A doctor has limited time and doesnât review the latest literature. A radiologist studies a scan for minutes instead of hours. A small business owner has no budget for a financial analyst.

When cognition costs approach zero, every curiosity can get a research team.

The amount of thinking done by machines will grow by orders of magnitude. Which raises the question, what will all that thinking be spent on?

The primal application of the Industrial Revolution was spinning textiles.

Sources indicate that spinning and weaving were skilled work. Textile makers were respected in your society: years of apprenticeship, a craft guild, a trade the family had held for generations. In 1764, James Hargreaves built the Spinning Jenny, which let one person spin eight threads at once, and later eighty. Clothing prices fell rapidly and global clothing consumption exploded.

Industry observers note that the big change was the human moving from performing the task to supervising it. One person tending a frame produced what a room of hand-spinners once had.

According to recent reports, the primal skilled application of this era is AI coding. Writing software is our era's elite craft: highly skilled, highly paid, a decade to master. And it is the first cognitive task where the pattern has fully flipped. The machine now completes most of the work, and the engineer's job is to direct, review and correct it. Itâs no accident that this is where the Cognitive Revolution found its first commercial traction.

While textiles kicked off the industrial revolution, they did not define it. The ultimate innovation of the industrial revolution was the automobile: a civilization grew around it, including suburbs, highways, supply chains, and the entire geography of modern life.

Coding agents are our Spinning Jennies: the first act, automating a skilled cognitive task. The automobile of this revolution has probably not been built yet. It will be something that was impossible while thinking was scarce.

My candidates: science conducted at machine speed, the personal agent that serves your life the way a chief of staff organizes a CEO's, or something in how humans connect and coordinate. In 1800, the automobile would have been hard to predict.

In 1800, over 75% of American workers worked the land. Machines came for that work. Today, farming is about 1% of U.S. employment. By the pessimists' arithmetic, over 74% of the country should be unemployed.

Instead we invented work no farmer in 1800 could have named. Radiologist. Software engineer. Podcast producer. Flight attendant. The machines did not end labor. They eliminated categories of work and expanded the total amount of it. There are more people employed today than at any point in human history, and they are vastly richer than their ancestors. All of my ancestors worked in agriculture 100 years ago. I knew all four of my grandparents, all of whom were born to farming families. None of them finished their lives in agriculture. All of them considered the non-agricultural work they did at the end of their lives more pleasant and prosperous than the hard agricultural work their families had done for generations.

Recent findings suggest that the same is taking shape in the Cognitive revolution. Despite the âspinning Jennyâ phenomena in AI coding, data supports that demand for software engineers, the most AI exposed occupation was accelerating higher, has inflected. In the coming week, we initiative to share data supporting inflections in hiring in other areas being transformed by AI, including Legal Services and Financial Services.

Machines doing cognitive work will not mean humans stop doing cognitive work any more than the tractor meant humans stopped doing physical things. The specific tasks change. The junior analyst who builds the model by hand becomes the person directing a hundred models. Further, categories of work we cannot currently name will grow the way "engineer" became a job following the invention of the engine during the Industrial Revolution.

Like in the industrial revolution, the aggregate story will be triumphant. But, the individual story will frequently not be. The handloom weavers of Lancashire were not retrained into locomotive engineers. Many of them simply lost, and their losses spanned a generation. The economic historian Robert Allen gave the period a name: Engels' pause. Between 1780 and 1840, British output per worker rose 46%. Real wages rose 12%.

Luddites were not wrong about their own lives, but about their childrenâs and grandchildren's. Between 1840 and 1900, British output per worker rose 90% and real wages rose 123%. Wages caught up to productivity, and then outran it.

It has been revealed that A pause is not a foregone conclusion. Mark Zuckerberg put this well recently: âThere is no rule that AI must increase automation faster than it increases individuals' capabilities or demand for upcoming skills.â Humanityâs demand for new skills, for better and worse, will be insatiable.The difference this time is speed. The Industrial Revolution gave a farmhand's son forty years to become a factory hand. This revolution may offer five. Society's shock absorbers, like education, retraining, and safety nets, were designed for the old clock. The central policy question of the next two decades is whether we can help humans transform as fast as the jobs do.

The Industrial Revolution created the modern education system, in at least two ways.

First, it made mass education possible. When most of humanity had to work the fields, children were labor. Machines taking over the physical work is what freed children to sit in classrooms and freed societies to fund them. The modern university exists because society no longer needed every able body in the field, and could redirect a civilization's youth toward cognitive skill-building instead.

Recent findings suggest that second, and less flatteringly, it shaped what education became. The factory needed workers who could read instructions, do arithmetic, show up on time and perform standardized tasks in synchronized shifts. So we built schools that look suspiciously like factories: Bells. Rows. Fixed schedules. Batch processing by age. Standardized outputs. Mass education was, in large part, industrial job training.

The Cognitive Revolution upends both of these dynamics. If machines do the cognition, the factory-model school is the equivalent of training for hand-spinning. But the deeper change is on the delivery side. For all of history, the binding constraint on education was the ratio of teachers to students. Benjamin Bloom quantified the cost of that constraint in 1984: the average student tutored one-to-one with mastery learning outperformed 98% of students in a conventional classroom.

Sources indicate that that constraint is dissolving. The marginal cost of an infinitely patient, endlessly knowledgeable tutor is approaching zero. Hybrid human-AI tutors are found to be more effective and less costly than traditional education. Further, new hybrid AI approaches could help spread education in parts of the world where public education has been prohibitively expensive.

In a recent development, modern medicine was also built by the industrial revolution. Mass production gave us penicillin at scale, refrigeration that made vaccines deliverable, and the chemical industry that spawned the pharmaceutical industry.

Recent findings suggest that the Cognitive Revolution pushes this much further. Drug discovery is a search across a space too large for humans to comprehend, which is exactly the work that scales best when cognition gets cheap. By predicting structures for virtually every known protein, AlphaFold solved a challenge where even minor breakthroughs previously demanded entire lifelong careers.Thousands of diseases right now have no treatment, not because they are unsolvable but because the cost of investigating each was never justified by the number of patients. When that cost collapses, the long tail becomes addressable the way every other latent demand does.

Curing disease has been the ambition of every generation of physicians. This is the first generation where the binding constraint is no longer how many of them there are.

Then there are the doctors in clinical practice. We face a massive shortage of physicians both in the United States and globally, with demand far exceeding supply. This problem is deeply personal to me, as I have long seen healthcare workers in my family stretched thin attempting to meet patient needs. Cheaper, accessible cognitive tools will not lead to doctors taking time off; instead, they will allow more patients to receive higher-quality care. Given the virtually limitless demand for better healthcare, scalable intelligence can help shift our medical model from reactive treatment to proactive care.The Shape of Daily Life.

Beyond work and school, the Industrial Revolution changed the texture of ordinary life so thoroughly that we now mistake its artifacts for human nature. The Cognitive Revolution will change them once again.

Clock time. Before factories, rural work followed seasons and sunlight. But a factory owner needed hundreds of people to start and stop simultaneously. The machine ran on a schedule, so the humans had to. Rigid shifts, the workday, the work week, modern timekeeping itself: these are industrial inventions, barely two centuries old. The Cognitive Revolution loosens their grip. When your machine colleagues work continuously and asynchronously, there is no reason for a hundred humans to think in unison from nine to five. Work drifts back toward task rhythms rather than clock rhythms.

According to recent reports, home and Work. Work happened in and around the home for most of human history: the farm, the cottage workshop, the family trade. Industrialization pulled the workplace out of domestic space because the work had to happen where the machine was. The daily commute is the residue of that separation. The Cognitive Revolution reverses it, because the machine now lives everywhere and one of the most powerful tools in history fits in your pocket. Home and work are recombining.

Global trade and power. Industrial nations imported raw materials and exported finished goods, an asymmetry that drove imperialism. The upcoming raw materials are energy, compute and algorithms. The finished good is intelligence. The last time this asymmetry appeared, it defined a century of international order and disorder: the same industrial base that laid rail and poured steel also eventually created atomic bombs. Intelligence will be dual-use in the same way, and faster. The Industrial Revolution lifted humanity, but its safeguards arrived late. This time we should try to be earlier.

Follow the thread and you eventually arrive at the real question underneath the anxiety about AI: If the machines do the thinking, what are we for?

Industry observers note that the last revolution already answered the physical version. At the end of the Industrial Revolution, humans did not stop moving their bodies. We remained embodied creatures.

According to recent reports, proportionally, fewer of us work intense physical jobs. However, far more of us move for sport and purpose: we run marathons, climb mountains, and pay for the privilege of holding yoga poses in uncomfortably hot rooms. Along the way, we created sports-leagues and even the modern Olympics were the result of the Industrial Revolution.

Cognition will make the same migration. Chess is a clean example. Deep Blue beat Garry Kasparov in 1997 and Kasparov later half-jokingly described himself as the first knowledge worker whose job was threatened by a machine. Chess did not die. More people play it today than at any point in history. When AlphaGo beat Lee Sedol, researchers found that the novelty of moves played by human Go professionals increased significantly afterward. Superhuman machines made human play more creative, not less. The âcentaurâ era of machine-human collaboration was brief, but the human era never ended.

Recent findings suggest that critics of this essay will argue that âthis time is different.â Specifically, they will point out that humans were the smartest animals on earth and that this is the first time something uniquely human is displaced by a machine. That is incorrect. It is incorrect for at least two reasons. First, thinking is not uniquely human. Animals think. Even nature follows complex and âintelligentâ patterns. Second, there are many uniquely human skills that machines exceed already. For example, making fire is strictly a human skillâ¦and now your stove does it with the press of a button. Same with writing and transferring information (the internet). Same with making tools (us and chimpanzees), but now machines make most of our tools. And then Einstein reinvented it completely-- humans making a comeback -- with a new human thought experiment that was needed to accurately plot the orbit of Mercury! Flight was a super-human task until airplanes made it accessible. This time is different, but not that different.What stays economically human the longest is what was never really cognition to begin with: wanting things, choosing between them, being accountable for the choice, and being trusted by other people. The machine can draft the treaty. Someone still has to sign it. Over 2500 years ago, Greek philosopher Protagaros wrote "Man is the measure of all things." Indeed, value as we experience it is in what we offer to other people.

Stand far enough back and this is all one story. For all of history, humans did the work: with our muscles and with our minds. Twice, we built machines that took the work and externalized it to machines.

The first time, we were terrified, and the fear was short-term justified and long-term wrong. The world after the machines took most of the physical work was profoundly more abundant, healthy  and humane.

Sources indicate that the same trade is on the table now, at greater scale and higher speed. The Cognitive Revolution will be turbulent, unevenly distributed, and deeply uncomfortable . And, it will end the way the last one did: with the world unrecognizably better, its results so completely woven into daily life that our grandchildren will live inside them.

We have made this trip before.This time, we can navigate it with our eyes open: shaping the transition calmly, sharing the prosperity, and remembering that the goal of externalizing our minds is ultimately to elevate our humanity.

Latest Update: As decision model use skyrockets, is customization the next frontier?

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (766 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: TechCrunch

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In October, more than one in four requests on Vercel’s AI model router went to decision models, not LLMs — an enormous share of work for a kind of computerized intelligence that was invented only a month earlier.
  • Industry observers note that decision models are LLMs that don’t produce output tokens; instead, they’re tuned to use their general intelligence to promptly and cheaply decide between preset options, while registering its level of confidence in the choice.
  • TypeSafe became a $7.5 billion manufacturer after releasing its Jev family of models, which continues to dominate usage (at least where we can see metrics from services like OpenRouter, which handled more than 1.5 billion queries to TypeSafe’s models last week).
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In October, more than one in four requests on Vercel’s AI model router went to decision models, not LLMs — an enormous share of work for a kind of computerized intelligence that was invented only a month earlier.

Industry observers note that decision models are LLMs that don’t produce output tokens; instead, they’re tuned to use their general intelligence to promptly and cheaply decide between preset options, while registering its level of confidence in the choice. They’re useful in production environments, where fast decisions can be more important than the reasoning provided by a slower and more expensive frontier model.

TypeSafe became a $7.5 billion manufacturer after releasing its Jev family of models, which continues to dominate usage (at least where we can see metrics from services like OpenRouter, which handled more than 1.5 billion queries to TypeSafe’s models last week).

However, it’s easy to make a decision model, and dozens were released in the wake of Jev. One Amazon engineer made one in a weekend, and soon every hyperscaler had its own option. On Tuesday, Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella said that his tech giant is rolling out its decision model, Microsoft-Decision-1.1, for wide use on Azure immediately.

The action is happening on both ends of the ecosystem: Sqwish, a U.K.-based AI startup behind a decision model called kettei fat, revealed a $3 million pre-seed round today. Co-founders Ushnish Sengupta and Federica Freddi, who met as Cambridge grad students, had been developing small LLMs when Jev arrived on the scene, and they realized their architectures could be repurposed as a powerful decision model.

Industry observers note that data appears to be the key to a successful model in this category — TypeSafe CEO Diogo Almeida told TechCrunch that the hardest part of building Jev was finely calibrating its judgment using statistically-adjusted synthetic data. Sqwish, too, has been working with synthetic data, but its unique offering is built-in post-training tools that use a customer’s own data to improve the model’s judgment.

“What makes us not a commodity, I think, is the fact that we are offering our customers the same power…they can keep uploading their production data, and just the same way that we trained our models, their models can also keep getting better at the tasks that they care about,” CEO Ushnish Sengupta told TechCrunch.

Attempting to rank decision models is difficult; Sqwish’s “kettei fat” model has performed well on some benchmarks, but most builders of the technology say that the real proof is in the pudding: It’s generally simple for developers to sub in one model for another and see how it does in a specific context.

“The benchmark is more of an invitation to try the model out, and then the continual tuning is the reason why they should stick to us,” Sengupta said.

Recent findings suggest that the Microsoft-Decision-1.1 model is also the result of the organization carefully balancing across cost, latency, intelligence and calibration. Achint Srivastava, the engineering VP who led the project, agreed that too much focus on benchmarks is a mistake.

“What we see is that ‘benchmaxed’ models fall flat under real enterprise usage very quickly,” Srivastava wrote in an email. “Our testing underscores just how challenging it is to deliver accuracy, reliability, speed and cost efficiency in a single model. Microsoft-Decision-1.1 and Jev are among the few that perform strongly across all four dimensions, even when evaluated on ‘held out’ or unseen benchmarks reflective of real use cases.”.

It has been revealed that for startups like Sqwish, competition with hyperscalers and frontier labs is an opportunity. Freddi predicts that future systems will see so-called System One intelligence, like decision models, working in concert with System Two intelligence, like frontier LLMs.

“Even in that future, System One is maybe a $10 billion, $50 billion [opportunity], and OpenAI is doing this IPO with you know $1 trillion, $2 trillion market value in mind,” she told TechCrunch. “This is all we care about; whereas for them, this is just a side project.”.

#39724. Robo-soldier startup backed by Eric Trump misses payroll, may collapse

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (948 w)

Robo-soldier startup backed by Eric Trump misses payroll, may collapse

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (948 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Ars Technica

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A humanoid robotics tech giant backed and advised by President Donald Trump’s son, Eric Trump, has reportedly missed payroll and may be on the brink of collapse after a funding shortfall.
  • According to recent reports, foundation failed to pay employees for the payroll period ending on October 30, anonymous sources told CNBC.
  • This comes as Pathak and Foundation’s leadership are still looking to raise funding to support a $3 billion valuation, based on their promise to develop a humanoid robot ready for combat duty and capable of wielding various weapons.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A humanoid robotics tech giant backed and advised by President Donald Trump’s son, Eric Trump, has reportedly missed payroll and may be on the brink of collapse after a funding shortfall. The Silicon Valley startup, Foundation Future Industries, claims it is developing and testing robots for military roles on battlefields from Ukraine to Gaza.

According to recent reports, foundation failed to pay employees for the payroll period ending on October 30, anonymous sources told CNBC. The startup’s staff is especially angry because Foundation’s co-founder and CEO, Sankaet Pathak, supposedly borrowed $4.6 million in manufacturer funds to buy a luxury home overlooking San Francisco Bay about a year ago.

This comes as Pathak and Foundation’s leadership are still looking to raise funding to support a $3 billion valuation, based on their promise to develop a humanoid robot ready for combat duty and capable of wielding various weapons.

It has been revealed that the company has demonstrated a humanoid robot named the Phantom MK-1 and is touting an upcoming robot called the Phantom MK-2. Foundation has touted its humanoid robots for roles in warehouses and other workplaces—but has courted media coverage by claiming it is developing humanoid robots for battlefield use.

Now CNBC’s reporting based on “people with direct knowledge of the matter” indicates that insiders worry the startup could soon collapse without additional funding.

Sources indicate that eric Trump holds an equity stake in Foundation and was revealed as its chief strategy advisor in March 2026, according to the Financial Times. Investment funds linked to both Eric Trump and Donald Trump Jr. are involved with multiple military technology companies that have received Pentagon loans and contracts worth more than $3.2 billion as of July 2026, according to The Washington Post.

After Trump claimed that Foundation had “just secured a $24 million contract with the Pentagon” during the Fox Business interview in April, Sen. Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.) responded by questioning whether the Pentagon is “just a cash machine for Trump’s kids now” in a social media post. “This looks like corruption in plain sight,” Warren wrote.

In a recent development, but publicly available evidence does not back up Trump’s claim about Foundation directly receiving US government funding. Federal spending records show that Foundation holds no publicly listed contracts, according to The San Francisco Standard.

Instead, the organization Boardwalk Robotics received four contracts worth $3.22 million prior to being acquired by Foundation in late 2024.

Meanwhile, the Institute for Human & Machine Cognition—a Florida-based nonprofit research institute and research partner to Boardwalk Robotics—secured a $24.8 million Navy contract in 2025, The San Francisco Standard reported.

This was not the first time that Foundation’s leadership and investors have made unsupported statements. In 2024, General Motors pushed back on Foundation’s claims that it was about to get an investment from the Detroit automaker, according to CNBC.

Industry observers note that on November 11, 2026, Mike LeBlanc, co-founder and president of Foundation Future Industries, told the Financial Times that the organization was in talks with the Israeli military to provide humanoid robots for patrol and combat duties in Hamas tunnels beneath Gaza. He also described taking the company’s Phantom MK1 humanoid robot along to tour some of the tunnels.

However, the Israeli defense ministry declined to comment when the Financial Times reached out.

LeBlanc also previously claimed that two of the manufacturer’s Phantom MK-1 units went to Ukraine for testing in frontline reconnaissance and logistics roles in February 2026.

But Craig Smith, an independent journalist and host of the podcast Eye on AI, described tagging along during the delivery of the Phantom robots to Ukraine. He noted that the robots never made it to Ukraine because they were stopped at the border with Poland.

According to recent reports, when questioned by Smith, LeBlanc only said that Foundation had conducted a pilot demonstration at an undisclosed location, without clarifying whether the robots ever reached Ukraine. LeBlanc also walked back a claim that Foundation had demonstrated its humanoid robots to the Ukrainian government organization Brave1.

Sources indicate that promotional videos showing Foundation’s humanoids have not provided evidence that the robots are ready for battlefield deployments. For example, a “mortar demo” video on the tech giant website dated to May 2026 reveals a person handing a mortar shell to one of the humanoid robots, which slowly lowers the shell over the muzzle of a mortar weapon before finally dropping it in.

Whatever happens to Foundation, humanoid robots remain largely unproven technology and have yet to fulfill company promises that they can become general-purpose robots handling many different tasks. Companies have just begun testing and deploying such robots in greater numbers within relatively controlled environments such as factories and warehouses.

Similarly, humanoid robots have not yet had any impact on the battlefield. Instead, pioneers in robotics warfare, like the Ukrainian military, have focused on developing and deploying unmanned ground vehicles (UGVs)—robotic vehicles that roll along on wheels or tank-style caterpillar tracks.

Sources indicate that while defending against the Russian invasion of Ukraine, the Ukrainian military has increasingly deployed more ground robots along with swarms of flying drones to make up for a shortfall in human soldiers compared to Russia. Such ground robots have typically been tasked with performing risky supply runs or evacuating wounded soldiers from frontline positions, but have also entered combat while wielding projectile weapons or even explosives when equipped as roving bombs.

Recent findings suggest that most recently, Ukraine has deployed armed ground robots directly into combat through both amphibious landings and through airdrops. In 2026, part of Ukraine’s counteroffensive success in rolling back Russian territorial gains has included dropping military robots from drones in airborne assaults behind Russian frontline positions.

#39718. Apple HomeView Review (2026): Should’ve Been Better

📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1812 w)
📖 Baca
Gadgets ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 WIRED ↗ Open Full Page

Apple HomeView Review (2026): Should’ve Been Better

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1812 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: WIRED

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • I never thought Apple would launch a smart display.
  • In a recent development, apple has been historically late to the game in the smart-home world, if it bothers showing up at all.
  • Industry observers note that with the HomeView's arrival, Apple is making its first foray into the smart display category, nearly 10 years after Amazon’s first Echo Show model.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

I never thought Apple would launch a smart display.

In a recent development, apple has been historically late to the game in the smart-home world, if it bothers showing up at all. It’s had the most minimal smart speaker (and general smart home) offerings of any of the major brands, with just the HomePod and HomePod mini compared with the variety of speakers and smart home products Amazon and Google have introduced in the past decade. A limited selection isn't necessarily a bad thing, but the Apple HomePods have also never excelled in our testing, either, and Apple's overall ecosystem has had the most limited compatibility compared with other devices (though Matter is helping expand that).

Industry observers note that with the HomeView's arrival, Apple is making its first foray into the smart display category, nearly 10 years after Amazon’s first Echo Show model. While the HomeView manages to do some things well, it's once again a product made for only the biggest of Apple enthusiasts, and will shine best for users who have an iCloud subscription, love Apple Music, and will invest in Apple’s upcoming, larger smart-home ecosystem, which has been designed in collaboration with LG and Schneider Electric. The HomeView does feel handy to use for making calls and sending texts—more so than any Amazon Echo Show ever was—and I love that I can use it to find my iPhone when I lose it around the house.

Still, I'd love to have been more impressed at this price point. After nearly two weeks of using the HomeView in my house, I find I use it most as a smart-home controller and to answer quick questions, and occasionally to FaceTime someone. Siri struggled to complete some of my music requests and took a long time to think about simple questions. Plus, some features on the device overall were roadblocked by my not having a full commitment to iCloud and Apple Photos. It's a device primarily for Apple devotees—especially the ones who will buy all of Apple's new smart-home products.

In a recent development, the most surprising thing to me is how small this device is. Maybe I've been overly influenced by the announcement of Amazon’s Echo Show 16, which has a generous 16-inch display (hence the name), but the HomeView screen is just 7 inches and square, giving it a different look from most other smart displays, which go for a rectangular design. My colleague Julian Chokkattu described it as a “giant Apple Watch,” and I agree. The swiping side to side to switch between 10 different preloaded faces and the menu bar also feel incredibly similar to the Apple Watch.

Industry observers note that pressing and holding on the face of the HomeView allows you to customize your various “faces” (or remove them—it's a lot of options to have preloaded, in my opinion, and I found myself swiping through too frequently to find the smart home page). You can also click on the plus button to add other faces or informational pages like weather and views of your home cameras. But that's all you can add, at least for now. There's no app store, but the device can reflect certain apps from your phone, along with general apps you'd find on an Apple device like Safari, FaceTime, Messages, Find My, Alarms, and more. I was surprised to see Spotify, Libby, and Yoto specifically ported over from my phone, but no other non-Apple apps have made it over so far, at least from my own collection of downloaded apps.

There isn't a Siri AI app on the HomeView like on my iPhone, but the HomeView does use Siri AI to power its intelligence and answer your questions. You'll get a more conversational response than regular Siri, but I didn't find its answers to be that much more impressive. Siri ran into issues playing my music—it asks me whether the music should come from Books, TikTok, or Spotify if I don't specify, and then most of the time it still can't play the song on Spotify, even with my account set up. It also couldn't use Find My to find my iPhone when I asked. Both of these applications worked perfectly fine on the HomeView screen itself, but the on-device Siri isn't blowing me away thus far.

Industry observers note that in fact, most things worked better by touch than voice. Spotify voice requests didn't seem to work, but the Spotify app on the device worked fine, as did using the handoff feature to send Spotify music from my phone to the HomeView. The Find My feature also didn't work over voice command—when I called my phone the same name I had seen it referred to on the HomeView while playing music, it claimed I had no device under that name. However, tapping the Find My app on the HomeView let me find my phone in a list of devices and tap it to make it start going off. While I'm bummed Siri won't let me just voice-request it, I am thrilled to have a faster way to find my iPhone lost in my house than pulling up iCloud.com.

Industry observers note that I tested the HomeView with both an iPhone Air and an older iPhone 16 Pro, but you'll want a newer phone like the Air (or 17 Pro, 18 Pro, or iPhone Duo) to get the most out of HomeView and Siri, since that's what gives you access to the expressive, customizable Siri voices. Switching to my original phone left me stuck with a boring Siri voice that I can't customize like I could when using the iPhone Air. No matter which phone you use, you'll also need to revision your phone's operating system to OS 27.2.1 in order to set up and connect to the HomeView (which also brings Siri AI onto your phone, much to my husband's chagrin).

In a recent development, the main appeal of the HomeView, at least in my opinion, is the fact that it can control your smart-home devices with touch or voice. This is especially relevant since Apple is rolling out a larger smart-home ecosystem, with several devices coming later this year as part of its Apple Home Collection, including indoor and outdoor cameras, a smart thermostat, a video doorbell, a smart lock, and a couple of sensors. You can already control any Apple Home–compatible device on the HomeView, though, without needing Apple's lineup to release.

The HomeView provides a similar experience to other smart displays, with a page you can swipe to for accessing all of the devices set up through your Apple Home app. It's easy to see the devices and quickly control them. Apple Home's biggest problem, though, continues to be compatibility. Many smart devices are only Amazon- and Google-compatible, though Matter is fixing some of that issue; I was able to connect the Ikea Varmblixt ($100) smart lamp to my Apple Home app thanks to the Matter compatibility. It was fast and seamless to control once set up, both over voice and touch.

It has been revealed that you can also touch to access your texts and FaceTime your contacts with the HomeView, which has been a pretty smooth experience for me. What's most interesting, though, is how the HomeView will verify that it's only you looking at your text messages. If it sees that someone else in your family is trying to look at or access your texts, it'll prompt that family member to switch over to their own account. It only works if they're alone in range of the device's camera, though; if they're peeking over your shoulder, access won't be denied.

Apple isn't using FaceID for this, surprisingly enough. It uses biometric data to figure out who's asking via a protected part of the processor Apple calls the Secure Exclave. It's a newly introduced technology that's also on the Apple Watch; we'll have to see how it pans out in real time.

Of course, we can't talk about a smart display and speaker without talking about one of the key features: the speaker.

Sound is a significant part of the enjoyment from this device, and while I enjoyed the audio quality, I found it frustrating to voice-request a song. When I asked for music without prompting which app it should come from, Siri asked me if I'd like it to come from Books, TikTok, or Spotify. And when I would request a song on Spotify, Siri would say I needed to “unlock my device,” but didn't specify if that needed to happen on my iPhone or my HomeView. Or it would simply tell me there was a problem and tell me to try again.

This is a huge bummer for my day-to-day use: I have a 4-year-old who loves making his own music requests and has gotten excellent at asking Google to play his latest favorite song (we're finally coming off of him requesting “Ghostbusters” and "This Is Halloween" on a daily basis).

Ultimately, the easiest way to play music as a Spotify user was using the handoff feature. The HomeView has a proximity-sharing feature similar to when you tap two iPhones to AirDrop a photo or other information, and it was much, much easier to pull up a song on my iPhone and simply place it near the HomeView to send what I was listening to to the speaker. I did really like that experience, but I think Spotify users will prefer other smart speakers if music playback is a primary feature they’re looking for.

Industry observers note that the sound itself was pretty good; I was happy jamming from a range of music, whether an autumn lo-fi mix or “The Call of the Mountains,” by Eluveitie. My long-time favorite song, “Dark Blue,” by Jack's Mannequin, sounded as clear with its piano keys and background drums as it did back in 2007 when I first started listening to it. The HomeView’s audio comes from the cylinder-like base that's only about 3 inches wide, giving it a slimmer profile than most smart display bases and even just stand-alone small smart speakers (the Google Home Speaker is about 5 inches at its widest point, for comparison). Inside that base sit two full-range drivers, a down-firing woofer that promises Spatial Audio, and two force-canceling passive radiators to build out the sound.

So, would I tell you to buy this? Only if you're a total Apple devotee who would use all of your preferred, Apple-run apps in tandem with the Apple HomeView. But it's really best if you're looking to invest in an Apple-run smart home (or already have one) and want a touchscreen to control it with. Or love FaceTiming so much you want an extra device for it. Otherwise, you'd be just as happy with cheaper smart displays or a simple smart speaker.

  • The change, which will roll out globally in the Gemini app over the coming weeks, marks a significant increase from the previous 72-hour retention period mentioned in Google’s Gemini Apps Privacy Hub, according to an archived version from November 12.
  • OpenAI, by comparison, states it may keep temporary chats in ChatGPT for up to 30 days, whereas Anthropic retains incognito chats in Claude for 30 days by default.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Google is extending how long it keeps temporary Gemini chats and conversations made with chat history turned off to around two months, saying the change aims to improve safety and security as AI systems become more capable.

The change, which will roll out globally in the Gemini app over the coming weeks, marks a significant increase from the previous 72-hour retention period mentioned in Google’s Gemini Apps Privacy Hub, according to an archived version from November 12.

OpenAI, by comparison, states it may keep temporary chats in ChatGPT for up to 30 days, whereas Anthropic retains incognito chats in Claude for 30 days by default. However, companies may keep some data longer for legal or safety reasons, or to investigate policy violations.

Google did not answer questions about what prompted the change and whether it would affect how conversations are accessed or reviewed, instead pointing to a blog post that claims chats are kept longer to respond to users, process feedback, and protect its services and users. Its updated Gemini Apps Privacy Hub also cites potential system failures as a reason for retaining chats and says temporary conversations are not used to train AI models.

The longer retention period comes as Google introduces separate settings for Gemini’s chat history and AI training. Until now, both were tied to a single “Keep Activity” setting. Owners will now be able to keep their conversations in their chat history without using them to train Google’s generative AI models.

Google indicates both upcoming settings will be turned off by default for consumers who previously disabled Keep Activity. For those who had Keep Activity turned on, their chat history will remain enabled. They can, though, decide separately whether Google can use their conversations to train AI models.

#39713. A Closer Look at Phonon TTS. Launching High-Quality On-Device Speech That Tops the Benchmarks.

📅 05 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1387 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Hugging Face ↗ Open Full Page

A Closer Look at Phonon TTS. Launching High-Quality On-Device Speech That Tops the Benchmarks.

📅 05 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1387 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Two weeks ago, we opened up Phonon, our small text-to-speech model that runs on your own device.
  • Sources indicate that we've been very happy with the reception so far.
  • Most voice AI lives in the cloud: every sentence makes a round trip to a server.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Two weeks ago, we opened up Phonon, our small text-to-speech model that runs on your own device. It needs no server and no network, and what you type stays with you.

Sources indicate that we've been very happy with the reception so far. So here's the story of the launch: why we built Phonon, what it can do, the demos that came with it, and how it did on Hugging Face's Open TTS Leaderboard.

Most voice AI lives in the cloud: every sentence makes a round trip to a server. Phonon runs on your own device instead. Your text stays there and the voice works without a network. We’ve also opened the weights. Phonon 31m is Apache 2.0, so you can use it for free, even in a commercial product. The other models are CC BY-NC, so they’re free for non-commercial projects. If you’re building something commercial with those, pricing is based on your number of users, not how much speech you generate.

Industry observers note that getting a good voice to run on a small device has always been hard. You could make the model small, but then it didn’t sound great. Or you could make it sound great, but then it wouldn’t fit. We addressed both.

According to recent reports, we confirmed Phonon in April and spent the next six months building on it with partners and early customers. Their feedback helped us to shape this release. The models got smaller, and we added more languages and support for custom voices through voice cloning and voice design.

Phonon is based on the Pocket TTS lineage and as such uses flow matching to generate the audio which is very different from the modeling techniques used in other TTS systems. This is what allowed us to bring this level of quality to such a small model but it created new challenges while training the models. The training was initially numerically unstable and required several tricks to produce quality results on all five languages.

Phonon comes in two sizes, at about 65 MB and 75 MB. Together they speak English, French, German, Spanish and Portuguese. There are more than 100 built-in voices, and you can create your own in Gradium Studio. Phonon also handles the important things that most other TTS systems often stumble on, like phone numbers, dates and codes.

It runs on phones, laptops, single-board computers and in a browser tab, so you can hear it right now. Phonon 31m speaks English and is Apache 2.0, so you can build on it freely, including for commercial products. Phonon 40m covers all five languages under a non-commercial license.

Recent findings suggest that the launch came with demos from friends and from our own team. On an Apple Watch with Wi-Fi off, Phonon talks you through a coffee brew step by step. On an iPhone with no signal, it counts your reps and keeps you going. A robot called Lamp, from Autonomous, wears a sorting hat and talks in character. In a browser, an offline dino runner becomes a radio show hosted by Rex. There's also a sci-fi game voiced on the player's own machine, and Proust read aloud page by page.

The Hugging Face team built the Transformers integration, so developers could use Phonon in Transformers from day one.

Sources indicate that developers have started building on it too. An ExecuTorch conversion runs Phonon on a visitor's GPU in the browser, Micdrop brings it to Node.js apps, and Spaces like smallest-s2s build on it.

Phonon was downloaded more than 200,000 times in its first two weeks, and it’s still trending on Hugging Face.

Recent findings suggest that the Open TTS Leaderboard is a very latest project from Hugging Face, and we love it. With more than 9,000 TTS models on the Hugging Face Hub, the leaderboard gives developers one place to compare open models and hear them side by side. Across 23 languages, models are evaluated on intelligibility (word error rate of the outputs), speed (inverse real-time factor and time-to-first audio), and naturalness (UTMOS for English and KOMOS for Korean). Fixed-voice and voice cloning are evaluated, with an additional speaker similarity metric for the latter. The leaderboard also has a Listen tab, where you can conveniently compare TTS outputs yourself and vote for the ones you like the most.

On intelligibility, Phonon ranks first in German and Spanish, and in the top three in every language we evaluated, next to models up to 100 times its size.

Speed is where we see Phonon truly shine, as the models top the CPU streaming benchmark on time-to-first audio.

It has been revealed that we built a fresh inference framework, ptts, specifically for Phonon. The goal of ptts is to get the best performance on a wide variety of devices and as such supports more than 10 backends: CPU (Intel, Arm, WebAssembly), GPU (CUDA, Vulkan, Metal, WebGPU), and NPU (Apple Core ML, Snapdragon®).

Sources indicate that phonon is also available in 🤗 Transformers, from v5.21, as its reference PyTorch implementation. Where ptts runs a single stream on device, Transformers targets GPU throughput: batched generation, full-graph torch.compile, e.g., for synthesizing speech datasets at scale. Being native PyTorch, it is a base to build upon, whether to integrate Phonon into your own stack or to study the model itself.

In a recent development, it belongs to the Pocket TTS lineage, so we first added Pocket TTS to Transformers. Phonon sits on top as a modular model: about 200 lines describing only what differs.

According to recent reports, phonon generates audio latents autoregressively: each step outputs a latent that is fed back as the next input, and the training loss is computed on them. Latents are the model's inputs, outputs and targets, as text tokens are for a language model, so the codec mapping audio to latents plays the role of a tokenizer. Transformers ships it as such: an audio tokenizer, held by the processor next to the text tokenizer:.

A voice is not a recording but a tensor of speaker latents. Phonon never encodes audio directly with its audio tokenizer, which ships decoder-only, and voices come precomputed: gradium/phonon-voices.

Sources indicate that the prompt layout (voice positions, text, then a token opening the audio) ships with the checkpoint as a chat template, as for other multimodal models in Transformers. You write a standard conversation, with an empty audio item where the voice goes, and your code stays the same across checkpoints. The processor then expands the voice placeholder to one position per frame, normalizes and tokenizes the text, and batches the inputs:.

generate returns latents, which the processor decodes to audio:.

Industry observers note that phonon can speak with any voice. Clone one from a short recording with the speaker’s consent, or describe a newly introduced one in plain text in Gradium Studio. Then download the voice file, load it in Phonon, and it runs fully on the device.

Industry observers note that we also train custom Phonon models with design partners. If your memory budget is tight, we can make the model smaller. If you need Korean, Arabic or Japanese, we can train for that too. And if your product has its own vocabulary, we can fine-tune on it. Get in touch and tell us what you need.

Thank you to the Hugging Face team, and to everyone who tried Phonon in its first two weeks.

It has been revealed that phonon is our first open release. Try it out and tell us what you build.

Recent findings suggest that congrats on the launch — running this cleanly on an Apple Watch with Wi-Fi off is genuinely impressive. As a German speaker I'm happy to see it top the intelligibility ranking in German; the compounding is unforgiving to TTS, so that's not a small win.

One line in "what's next" I keep coming back to: Korean, Arabic and Japanese get offered as custom-training requests. That framing quietly shows where the field's centre of gravity still sits — a handful of languages are first-class citizens, and everything else is a sales conversation. The Open TTS Leaderboard covering 23 languages is a great step, but the long tail of the world's languages is still waiting. Would love to see lower-resource languages get first-class leaderboard slots rather than a custom quote.

#39712. Artist brings old Space Shuttle tank back to life

📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1304 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Ars Technica ↗ Open Full Page

Artist brings old Space Shuttle tank back to life

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1304 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Ars Technica

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Natalie Rosen is not the type of specialist you immediately associate with being one of the key people behind the upcoming exhibit of the space shuttle Endeavour.
  • Recent findings suggest that she is not a former NASA technician or engineer, as many of her colleagues have been for the past several years, nor is she a curator or conservator.
  • Without her expertise and artistry, however, the largest component of Endeavour‘s “stack” would look nothing like it did when the shuttle was flying.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Natalie Rosen is not the type of specialist you immediately associate with being one of the key people behind the upcoming exhibit of the space shuttle Endeavour.

Recent findings suggest that she is not a former NASA technician or engineer, as many of her colleagues have been for the past several years, nor is she a curator or conservator. Before this job, she had no experience working on any aircraft or spacecraft, as the new Samuel Oschin Air and Space Center, an extension of the California Science Center, opened in Los Angeles on November 13.

Without her expertise and artistry, however, the largest component of Endeavour‘s “stack” would look nothing like it did when the shuttle was flying.

“My background is in the fine arts. I have my bachelor’s and my master’s in fine arts from Cal State Long Beach,” Rosen told collectSPACE.com. “When I came in on this project, they were looking for a sculptor, and I had been sculpting.”.

Industry observers note that rosen had been working with mixed media for her thesis project and had experience sculpting foam. As it happened, the California Science Center had a lot of foam that needed shaping.

Sources indicate that for those unfamiliar, the space shuttle was assembled from three primary launch components. The orbiter and its solid rocket boosters were reusable, given the time needed to inspect, service, and, in the case of the solid-fuel motors, refurbish and refill between flights.

Sources indicate that the 154-foot-tall (47-meter) external tank was the only major part of the stack that was disposed of with each launch. After providing propellant for the orbiter’s three main engines, the tank was jettisoned and disintegrated while reentering the atmosphere.

To protect the orbiter from the extreme cold of the cryogenic liquid oxygen and liquid hydrogen in the external tank and to keep the propellant and oxidizer from boiling off too quickly, the ET was covered in insulating foam. (Some of that foam became liberated during ascent and was what caused the loss of the space shuttle Columbia and its crew in 2003.).

According to recent reports, the only flight-worthy tank to remain at the end of the program was ET-94. A so-called lightweight tank, it was built at a time when NASA was transitioning to a super-lightweight model and was therefore set aside. Originally slated to support a science mission on Columbia, it instead became a testbed after the tragedy, having its foam stripped off and tested to better understand what had happened.

After the program ended, NASA donated ET-94 to the California Science Center. It arrived by way of a transoceanic barge and a road trip, then sat at Exposition Park for nearly a decade.

“So much of the foam on the ET had been dissected and removed during its time as a test article that they [the California Science Center] were trying to figure out how to put it back on and blend it in to the original foam in a convincing way,” stated Rosen.

There has been a longstanding debate among shuttle enthusiasts and modelers about exactly what color the external tank is, and the answer resides in the foam.

“It’s orange. It’s cream. It’s burnt sienna. It just depends on the original foam, when you’re seeing it and how it’s aging. Because it starts as a kind of very ice cream-white almost color, and then depending on how long it sits out in the Sun, it turns orange,” noted Rosen.

According to recent reports, by the time she had come on staff, the decision for the most part had already been made. Dennis Jenkins, the leader of the Endeavour project, had blended a special paint called “ET Orange” that was used to cover the existing acreage “bumpy” foam. Separately, a mocha-like color was picked out for the intertank.

Recent findings suggest that “And then the latest foam to be installed, which would have looked the newest on all of the closeout hardware—the feed lines, the ice frost ramps, the flanges around the intertank and the intertank rings—those were all the lightest color that we custom mixed. That was what we called the ice cream color,” Rosen noted.

It was not only about color matching, though. For multiple reasons, the original aerospace-grade foam could not be used, so a commercial substitute had to be found that could match what Rosen described as the “orange peel.”.

“If you look at the tank very closely, there’s this bumpy texture, and there is a pattern from the original manufacturing and how it was sprayed on. There’s this overlapping line, a subtle-like stripe to it,” she remarked.

Replicating that pattern was not easy.

It has been revealed that “There was a lot of trial and error in the beginning of what we could do to try and get it to match what was already there,” Rosen told collectSPACE. “We tried taking impressions off of the real foam and making molds and casting, but that didn’t really work. I then suggested we put in a dense urethane, like plain urethane foam, and I hand-sculpt the top of it to match what was around it. That ended up becoming the best solution for fixing the acreage foam that had an orange peel-like texture.”.

Jenkins, who had worked as a space shuttle engineer and led NASA’s delivery of the orbiters to their museum homes, had high praise for Rosen and her work.

“She had to come up with a lot of latest processes because we couldn’t apply foam the same way they did at Michoud. It’s not flightworthy by any means, but just coming up with how to make it look real took a lot of imagination on her part, and she was pretty much a one-woman show for most of it,” he remarked.

Some of the repair work to the external tank was finished before it was lifted by crane into the Samuel Oschin Air and Space Center and mated with the boosters and Endeavour. From then on, Rosen had to climb scaffolding to get to her worksites.

Recent findings suggest that “It’s definitely the largest art project I’ve ever worked on, and, I mean, I touched every inch of it,” Rosen stated. “Once it went vertical, I was going up and down stairs. Probably the scariest was the point in the scaffolding where it just became ladders. So I had to be very, very careful and calculated in what I was doing.”.

Recent findings suggest that even after the scaffolding was removed in preparation for the museum opening, Rosen’s ascents were not over. A couple of weeks ago, she had to install a final component on the aft dome of the liquid hydrogen tank. To reach that, she needed a scissor lift.

Industry observers note that now that the entire Endeavour stack has made its public debut, Rosen is not parting ways with the California Science Center. Her work on ET-94 has released her career into a new frontier.

In a recent development, “In this last year, I have been working on different artifacts with the team. I have been helping leading up to the opening. I’ve helped in ways with the different aircraft, with their assembly, their disassembly, and reassembly. I’ve done some repairs in certain areas. I’ve worked with our satellite and probe collection to do repairs and also contacted specialists outside of my realm to clean and repair thermal blankets,” stated Rosen.

Sources indicate that “So I’m planning on staying with the museum for now. They’ve offered me another position, and I’m happy to stay,” she noted.

The California Science Center’s Samuel Oschin Air and Space Center is now open to the public. Admission is free, but timed entry tickets are needed due to the high demand. Reservations can be made online or at 213-744-2019.

CISA Adds Two Known Exploited Vulnerabilities to Catalog

📅 29 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (462 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Cisa

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • CISA has added two newly introduced vulnerabilities to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) Catalog, based on evidence of active exploitation.
  • CISA has added two new vulnerabilities to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) Catalog, based on evidence of active exploitation.
  • These types of vulnerabilities are a frequent attack vector for malicious cyber actors and pose significant risks to the federal enterprise.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

CISA has added two newly introduced vulnerabilities to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) Catalog, based on evidence of active exploitation. CVE-2026-97229 GitLab Community Edition and Enterprise Edition Integer Overflow or Wraparound vulnerability CVE-2026-76418 Cisco Secure Firewall ASA Software and Cisco Secure FTD Software Unchecked Return Value to NULL Pointer Dereference Vulnerability These types of vulnerabilities are a frequent attack vector for malicious cyber actors and pose significant risks to the federal enterprise. Binding Operational Directive (BOD) 26-04: Prioritizing Security Updates Based on Risk establishes vulnerability management requirements for Federal Civilian Executive Branch (FCEB) agencies. BOD 26-04 reinforces the importance of the KEV Catalog and requires federal agencies to prioritize rapid remediation of high-risk vulnerabilities, specifically those identified by Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVEs) listed in CISA’s KEV Catalog on publicly exposed assets that grant total control of the asset post-exploitation, while deferring action for lower-risk vulnerabilities. BOD 26-04 further establishes basic expectations for when agencies must check whether threat actors compromised the system before the patch was applied. While BOD 26-04 applies only to FCEB agencies, CISA encourages all organizations to adopt risk-based vulnerability management and prioritize remediation of KEV Catalog vulnerabilities. CISA will continue to add vulnerabilities to the catalog that meet the specified criteria. Aware of an exploited vulnerability not right now listed in the KEV Catalog? Submit it for potential addition through CISA’s KEV Nomination Form. Potential KEV additions must have a CVE ID, evidence of exploitation, and clear mitigation guidance.

CISA has added two new vulnerabilities to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) Catalog, based on evidence of active exploitation.

These types of vulnerabilities are a frequent attack vector for malicious cyber actors and pose significant risks to the federal enterprise.

Binding Operational Directive (BOD) 26-04: Prioritizing Security Updates Based on Risk establishes vulnerability management requirements for Federal Civilian Executive Branch (FCEB) agencies. BOD 26-04 reinforces the importance of the KEV Catalog and requires federal agencies to prioritize rapid remediation of high-risk vulnerabilities, specifically those identified by Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVEs) listed in CISA’s KEV Catalog on publicly exposed assets that grant total control of the asset post-exploitation, while deferring action for lower-risk vulnerabilities. BOD 26-04 further establishes basic expectations for when agencies must check whether threat actors compromised the system before the patch was applied.

Sources indicate that while BOD 26-04 applies only to FCEB agencies, CISA encourages all organizations to adopt risk-based vulnerability management and prioritize remediation of KEV Catalog vulnerabilities. CISA will continue to add vulnerabilities to the catalog that meet the specified criteria.

Aware of an exploited vulnerability not currently listed in the KEV Catalog? Submit it for potential addition through CISA’s KEV Nomination Form. Potential KEV additions must have a CVE ID, evidence of exploitation, and clear mitigation guidance.

Industry observers note that controlling what AI agents can reach is one of the biggest constraints on enterprise AI adoption. Cymphony is building the governance and security layer that removes it.

Sources indicate that controlling what AI agents can reach is one of the biggest constraints on enterprise AI adoption. Cymphony is building the governance and security layer that removes it.

It has been revealed that every large enterprise now has an AI mandate. Very few know exactly what happens when an agent is granted access to enterprise systems and data. What exactly will it be able to reach? How will we know what it did with it? These questions â not model quality, not cost, not talent â are the reason so many enterprise AI programs stay stuck in pilots. Cymphony was built to answer them.

Sources indicate that employees increasingly work together with AI agents to execute day-to-day work. But the typical agent is nothing like an employee. It can be provisioned in minutes rather than hired over weeks. It works continuously. And it can reach across far more systems, data, and capability than an individual person. Every one of those properties is what makes an AI agent worth deploying â and every one of them is what makes a security team say no.

In a recent development, governance and security are already major barriers to AI adoption, with 40% of enterprises expected to demote or decommission autonomous AI agents over governance concerns by next year. That is not a prediction about AI failing to work. Itâs about enterprises pulling back working agents because they cannot see or control what those agents reaching. The fundamental challenge is not utility, but accountability.

According to recent reports, for decades, security teams have built tools around two separate concerns: where sensitive data lives, and who has access. The first produced the tools that watch files, inboxes, and databases for leaks. The second produced the identity industry. But both assume the "who"s are human employees.

AI broke that assumption. An identity tool can tell you an agent exists. A data tool can tell you a file is sensitive. Neither can tell you that a given agent, acting on behalf of a given employee, can reach that file right now. Identity security and data security are no longer separable.

Cymphony continuously maps both employees and agents across an enterprise, graphing who and what can reach which systems and information. It is a difficult engineering problem: the same person routinely holds a dozen different accounts scattered across systems that were never designed to talk to each other, and agents inherit access from the humans and applications that spawned them. Stitching all of that back into one accurate picture requires more than a dashboard that aggregates alerts.

What we love about working with co-founders Shy Dekel, Idan Berkovits, and Edi Gotlieb is their instinct to build not for the alert but for the workflow. Instead of stopping at detection and leaving a security analyst to figure out what to do next, Cymphony pushes further â recommending and even automating remediation, and coordinating with the people who need to take action.

Enterprise customers including Syngenta, KKR, Cass Information Systems, and Athennian are already seeing results. Sequoia is also a happy customer. We are proud to have led Cymphonyâs seed round, and to now co-lead their Series A.

We met Shy, Idan, and Edi through Sequoia's Israel network, introduced separately by two people in our orbit who each said some version of the same thing: these three had spent their careers on hard, unglamorous security problem many founders avoid, and they were building something different around it. All three came out of Israel's elite Talpiot program. All three have deep experience in this space: Shy led the cyber department for Unit 8200, Idan ran a research group in the Office of the Prime Minister and won an Israel Defense Prize, and Edi built hardware at Apple and at the Israeli Ministry of Defense. Every large enterprise software manufacturer has been built on a transition: the underlying unit of work changes, and the old categories are no longer the right shape. Cloud changed where software ran, and security rebuilt itself around it. Mobile changed what an endpoint was, and it rebuilt itself again. Each time, the companies that offered visibility and control over what came next eventually became infrastructure everyone else took for granted.

AI is no exception, albeit the first shift where the upcoming unit of work can act on its own. The organization that lets an enterprise say yes to agents â confidently, at scale, with a record of what they did â will be not just a feature inside the AI stack, but a precondition for it. We think Cymphony is building that layer, and we are glad to be part of it.

By Bogomil Balkansky, Dean Meyer and David Cahn.

After a recent slew of tech outages, service disruptions, and flight chaos this week, it’s now Apple customers who are facing technical challenges.

Sources indicate that the iPhone maker’s System Status page indicates that there are issues with iCloud’s Account & Sign In services affecting “all consumers,” which could make the service slow or unavailable. The App Store, AppleCare on Device, and Apple Music are also experiencing issues, the page indicates.

In a recent development, like all major tech companies, Apple faces outages and other technical challenges affecting its cloud services at times. However, today’s issues are likely more noticeable to end users because problems with iCloud can lead to account sign-in problems. This could cause your iPhone to ask for your Apple ID and password, and you could see other attempts to sign in to services with your Apple account information fail.

On Reddit, some folks also noted that they were unable to activate a new iPhone, which is likely related to these ongoing challenges.

Given the recent increase in AI-driven cyberattacks, consumers across social media have already begun to speculate about the cause. In particular, users are expressing concerns about the Apple outage, as it arrives only days after technical failures at Microsoft led to its cloud systems that power flagship services like Outlook and Teams failing due to cascading software complications.

Similarly, a brief outage of Chase’s banking app this week garnered attention, as did an ongoing partial outage (at the time of publication) of the National Security Agency’s internal classified network, both of which were blamed on software glitches.

So far, none of the outages in the past week have been attributed to cyberattacks, but rather to technical problems.

Industry observers note that apple responded to TechCrunch’s request for comment (which it initially gave to Bloomberg), noting that the outages were caused by an internal revision and not a cyberattack. “Many of our systems are back up and running after an internal update caused some outages this morning. We’re working to get the remaining systems online as soon as possible,” the statement read.

After the initial outages were reported, Apple’s status page was updated to include other outages impacting Apple School Manager, iCloud Mail, iCloud Web Apps (iCloud.com), Schoolwork, and the Volume Purchase Program.

By 6 PM ET on Tuesday, the status page showed all the outages were resolved.

#39703. Breaking: Grok Bot took unapproved actions, ignored orders to stop, and then denied it

📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (732 w)
